bikes.summary: Testers describe a smooth, linear 450 that builds power progressively and is easy to ride, though next to the Japanese 450s it can feel short on snap off the bottom. Handling is rated accurate and stable, but the stock air fork and rigid clamps draw complaints about harshness, while tuners also find the stock air setting too soft for fast riders. The 2021 fork update made the frame feel less rigid and the 2021 maps became easier to tell apart. Most fixes are about adding low-end response (exhaust flange, ECU, race fuel) and taking harshness out of the front end.

points.statement: Engine builds power smoothly and linearly from low to high rpm, which makes it easy and tiring-free to ride.
Low-end hit is mild; next to Japanese 450s it can feel sleepy and testers wanted more response and snap off corners.
For 2021 the two maps became easier to tell apart, with the aggressive map adding mid and top power rather than sharper throttle response.
Accurate and stable, needing little steering input; rated the best all-round handler of its years.
Frame is on the stiff side, which faster riders like more than vets; the 2021 fork update made the chassis feel less rigid.
Stock air fork and rigid stock clamps feel harsh, especially mid-stroke on braking bumps, and pass vibration to the hands.
Stock and recommended air settings are too soft for fast riders on rough tracks; tuners run more air or revalve.
Air pressure climbs on hot days (about 10 psi from morning to race time), so the fork must be checked and bled every moto.
Rear sits low under acceleration and feels harsh off corners; stock shock fades when hot late in long motos.
Hardware needs regular checks: rear sprocket bolts, spokes by the rim lock, head-stay and engine-mount bolts, shift lever and linkage nut.
Neutral is hard to find when stopped; easiest method is selecting it as revs drop with the clutch in.
Runs hot in hot conditions.

common_fixes.problem: Engine smooth but lacks low-end snap
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket exhaust flange (no remap)
common_fixes.result: Better mid-to-exit response and third-gear lugging

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket ECU with tuner maps
common_fixes.result: Stronger corner exits and could hold third longer

common_fixes.fix: Oxygenated race fuel on the stock map
common_fixes.result: More low-end pull and response within a few laps

common_fixes.fix: Split triple clamps with more flex
common_fixes.result: More comfort and front contact while staying precise in ruts

common_fixes.problem: Rear harsh under squat on square edges
common_fixes.fix: Floating axle blocks with a different axle
common_fixes.result: More compliance and traction; allowed stiffer low-speed compression

common_fixes.problem: Rear sits low and harsh on corner exits
common_fixes.fix: Shock shaft 1 mm longer and a slightly longer pull rod
common_fixes.result: Rear stayed higher, sag could return to 103-105 mm and the bike balanced

common_fixes.problem: Setup too soft for fast riders
common_fixes.fix: Stiffer mid-valve and low-speed stack, shock bladder, progressive linkage
common_fixes.result: More control and hold-up at some cost to initial plushness

common_fixes.fix: Vented airbox cover
common_fixes.result: About 1 hp more near peak on the dyno; use the solid cover in mud or dust

sides: Feels harsh in mid-stroke and over braking bumps
Stock and recommended settings are too soft for fast riders

bikes.generation: 2023+ generation (new engine and frame; flexier frame from 2025)
bikes.summary: Testers agree the current 450 SX-F engine is one of the strongest in the class yet broad and easy to use, with power building steadily from low rpm to a strong mid and top. The 2023-2024 chassis was widely criticised as stiff and harsh until well broken in, and the 2025 frame, linkage and mount changes are credited with making it more compliant and stable. The stock air fork gets mixed reviews: comfortable to some, harsh on small braking bumps or limiting at a high level to others, and the shock can go deep and bottom hard. Owners and tuners lean toward coil conversions, aftermarket linkages, softer engine mounts and clamps, and careful chain slack and pivot torque.

points.statement: Broad, linear power that is very strong from the middle to the top but still easy to manage in tight turns or a high gear.
Measures among the most powerful stock 450s on the dyno.
Off-idle and low-end feel is criticised: one tester found the early stock map jerky at low rpm with a hit that upset the bike in ruts, another found less low-end intensity than the Japanese 450s.
Strong engine braking and noticeable high-rpm vibration through stiff bars.
Quickshifter helps on long starts but feels quirky at half throttle and on jump faces, so some riders leave it off.
Traction control is mainly useful on hard, slick or wet tracks and adds little in loam.
The 2023-2024 frame feels stiff and harsh, deflects over braking bumps and needs roughly 8-10 hours to settle; it also feels heavier at the front.
From 2025 the chassis is more compliant in rough ground while staying stable and accurate, with no head shake and good rear traction.
Air fork is harsh on small braking bumps and its pressure drifts, hurting consistency; a harsh spot in mid-stroke is a common complaint.
Once broken in, testers run more fork air than the stock setting (around 10.8-10.9 bar) because the stock setting feels too soft.
Shock can go too deep in its stroke and bottom hard at the end, and may kick sideways on big hits.
2025 linkage and frame give more rear feedback, compliance and traction.
Cockpit feels cramped and the seat tall for short riders; shock clickers sit hidden behind the side panel.
Brakes are powerful.
Spokes near the rear rim lock loosen often; check before every ride.
Chain slack should be kept around 68-70 mm; tighter chains eat the swingarm buffer pad and load the suspension.
Linkage needle bearings can walk out and bind; 2023 start/stop switch could let water short the ECU; rear brake pedal tip bends easily (strengthened for 2025).
Aftermarket full exhaust systems add mid-to-top pull but soften or slightly reduce the low-end hit.
Places in the top three of 450 shootouts.

common_fixes.fix: Coil cartridge conversion (for example a valved WP 6500 kit) or lighter spring plus air with reduced damping
common_fixes.result: More comfort, lean traction and consistency; valved coil kits named as the biggest single fix

common_fixes.problem: AER soft once broken in but harsh with more air
common_fixes.fix: Raise fork oil level and lower air pressure
common_fixes.result: Hold-up without the harshness of simply adding air

common_fixes.problem: Rear goes deep and kicks on big bumps
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket linkage (softer initial, more progression, rear about 5 mm higher)
common_fixes.result: Calmer rear with better traction

common_fixes.fix: Medium-flex engine mounts, 23.5 mm offset split clamps, flexier bar, swingarm pivot at 95 Nm
common_fixes.result: Less slap-down harshness and vibration, better lean grip and less deflection

common_fixes.problem: Stock map jerky off idle / wants more pull
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket ECU or reprogrammed ECU with per-gear mapping
common_fixes.result: Smoother low end, stronger mid-top and less engine braking

common_fixes.fix: Replace needle bearings with caged KTM bearing 58033097000
common_fixes.result: Linkage moves freely again

sides: Aggressive map 2 (2023-2024 race tests, one 2024 dyno tester)
Mellow map 1 (2025-2026 race tests, one 2023 launch test)

disagreements.topic: Stock air fork on the 2026 bike
sides: Comfortable, resists bottoming and is balanced
Holds the bike back at the top level

bikes.summary: Testers describe the FC 450 as smooth and soft off the bottom, building predictably and deceptively fast, with a restrictive intake that makes it more lethargic than the KTM. The 2021 lowered chassis turns very well and is rated a top handler, but one tester found it unbalanced and harsh on chop, and the stock shock spring soft for heavier riders. The stock air fork drew repeated complaints about harshness and inconsistency, with sticker settings too soft. Cheap intake mods, linkage changes and brake-pedal spring fixes are common.

points.statement: Soft off the bottom, then builds predictably and linearly with no surges; deceptively fast, but less exciting than the KTM 450.
The 2020 ECU cured the rich-low, lean-top feel of the 2019; the 2020 Rockstar Edition ECU adds low-rpm response and cuts engine braking.
The 2021-2022 lowered chassis corners very well and feels smaller; rated better turning than the KTM 450.
The lowered 2021 chassis can feel unbalanced with the rear lower than the front, harsh on chop, and the frame can touch rut walls.
Stock air fork harsh and inconsistent through a moto; sticker settings too soft for a 190 lb rider.
Shock spring too soft for heavier riders: squats mid-corner and blows through in whoops.
Stock rear rigid on acceleration chop and kicks on decel bumps.
22 mm offset clamps were the best all-round choice; 20 mm turns in easier but hunts on throttle; 24 mm is most stable but lazy.
Rear brake pedal return spring breaks every 4-5 hours, stock bar mounts bend, and throttle cables wear by about 20 hours.
2022 composite subframes cracked at the lower right bolt hole and the fuel quick-release O-ring can tear.

common_fixes.fix: Screenless two-stroke filter cage or cutting out the backfire screen; exhaust flange
common_fixes.result: More low-end response for little money

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket linkage (different pull rod and knuckle)
common_fixes.result: Rear raised and the bike balanced

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket linkage with 48 N/mm spring, 103 mm sag
common_fixes.result: Rode higher with more traction and control on braking bumps

common_fixes.fix: Hybrid coil/air fork conversion or revalve
common_fixes.result: Spring-fork small-bump comfort with air-fork bottoming resistance

common_fixes.fix: Honda CRF450R rubber-covered spring or aftermarket return spring kit
common_fixes.result: Spring no longer breaks

common_fixes.problem: Chassis stiff when leaning on the throttle
common_fixes.fix: Remove one upper engine-mount bolt, torque others to 30 Nm; pivot at 95 Nm
common_fixes.result: More flex; can be too flexy in deep tilled dirt

common_fixes.fix: High-speed compression in 1/4 turn and sag kept near 95-105 mm
common_fixes.result: Calmer rear without hurting the fork

bikes.generation: 2023+ generation (lowered version of the KTM platform; no 2026 US model)
bikes.summary: The current FC 450 shares the KTM engine but its closed-off airbox gives a smoother, softer low end; testers still rate it the strongest or among the strongest 450s and very manageable. Its lower chassis earns praise for cornering, stability and fitting shorter riders. The weak spot testers keep finding is the rear: it rides low and deep, can bottom on big hits and the stock spring feels soft for heavier or faster riders. The air fork works but divides riders and needs setup knowledge.

points.statement: Among the most powerful 450s yet broad and manageable even for less skilled riders.
Closed-off airbox makes it smoother and mellower low-to-mid than the KTM, which feels brisker.
Low ride height helps it carve flat turns and ruts with excellent traction while staying stable and accurate.
About an inch lower than the KTM; suits short riders without bothering tall ones.
Rear rides low and deep: it squats mid-corner, can feel harsh and bottoms on landings or big hits, and the stock spring is soft for heavier or fast riders.
Air fork works but is setup-sensitive and divides riders.
The 2025 frame no longer needs a long break-in and feels plusher.
Powerful one-finger front brake with wide modulation.
Needs about 70 mm chain slack; spokes near the rim lock loosen; shroud blocks the shock clickers.
Special-edition titanium slip-on gave no peak power gain over the standard bike on one dyno.

common_fixes.fix: Stiffer shock spring (48 N/mm over about 190 lb), or slide forks out in the clamps and reduce sag
common_fixes.result: Rear sits higher and stops blowing through; clickers alone were only a stopgap

common_fixes.problem: Shock bottoms at end of stroke
common_fixes.fix: About five more clicks of low-speed compression
common_fixes.result: Helped control bottoming

common_fixes.problem: Slow throttle response from closed airbox
common_fixes.fix: Vented airbox cover
common_fixes.result: Sharper response

common_fixes.fix: Cut an access hole in the shroud
common_fixes.result: Clickers reachable without removing plastics

sides: Rear is excellent / chassis plusher
Rear rides low, harsh and bottoms on big hits

bikes.summary: Only one early first ride exists. Testers found it smooth on the first part of the throttle and then strong, physically demanding, and less settled on rough ground unless ridden fast and committed.

points.statement: Smooth on the first part of the throttle, then builds strongly; the most physically demanding bike in the range.
Less settled on rough ground unless ridden at a fast, committed pace.

bikes.summary: The first GasGas MC 450F is a KTM 450 SX-F engine and frame with cheaper parts and restrictions: a nearly sealed airbox cover, a header with no resonance chamber, muffler restrictors and no map switch. Testers consistently find it weaker and less racy off the bottom than the KTM, though it builds well through the middle and its peak power is competitive. Forged clamps and softer valving make it comfortable but vaguer to steer and too soft for fast riders.

points.statement: Weaker and less racy off the bottom than the KTM because of the sealed airbox, plain header and muffler restrictors.
Builds strongly through the middle; peak power is close to the KTM and competitive with rival 450s.
No handlebar map switch: it runs the mellow map only until an accessory switch is fitted.
Forged clamps flex more than billet ones: comfortable in rough ground but vague at turn-in, with tip-in oversteer then mid-corner push.
Softer valving than the KTM: too soft for fast riders and felt poor for the first few hours.
Rim-lock spokes loosen quickly; about half the test bikes had one loose.

common_fixes.fix: Cut the winglet off the airbox cover or fit a KTM vented cover
common_fixes.result: Better breathing and bottom-to-mid pull

common_fixes.fix: Clamp pinch bolts 20 Nm top, 15 Nm bottom, or billet clamps
common_fixes.result: Sharper steering

common_fixes.fix: Plug in the KTM map switch (about $180)
common_fixes.result: Access to map 2, traction and launch control

sides: Race test says the GasGas shares the KTM's Brembo brakes
Later recall notices cover Braktec front calipers on 2022 GasGas MCs

bikes.summary: On the current KTM platform the MC 450F is the mellow, budget sibling: testers find it fun and easy, but its closed airbox, restricted exhaust and single stock map blunt response and top-end pull, and it measures a bit below the KTM on the dyno. Softer valving and forged clamps make it compliant, so testers run more fork air than on the KTM. Opinions split on its Braktec brakes and on whether the fork is comfortable or harsh.

points.statement: Closed airbox, restricted muffler and the single stock map blunt response and top-end pull; it measures slightly below the KTM on the same dyno.
Mellow and fun with usable power everywhere; testers often ride it harder than the stronger KTM.
Valving is softer than the KTM's, so testers add fork air (around 10.6-10.9 bar).
2024 chassis changes direction and cuts under ruts easily.
Stock Maxxis tires lack side-knob grip.
Torque values printed on key bolts, few bolt lengths and one Torx size for bodywork.

common_fixes.fix: Drill or replace the airbox cover and fit the accessory map switch
common_fixes.result: Sharper response and access to the aggressive map

sides: Strong with no fade even for a brake dragger
Less power and feel than Brembo
Softer and compliant
Needs constant adjusting and harsh on small and big hits
Slightly more compliant than the KTM
Cast clamp and bars pass excess feedback

bikes.summary: Testers describe the previous-generation 350 SX-F as an engine that picks up quickly, pulls steadily and must be revved further than riders expect, yet can also be short-shifted like a 450. The 2021 aggressive map added midrange but felt less crisp than the 450's. In deep sand the stock air-fork setup rides deep and pitches, so testers and owners add compression and fine-tune air and sag. Small annoyances include a long-throw throttle cam, hard-to-find neutral and electrical niggles on 2022 bikes.

points.statement: Flexible engine: it rewards revving well past where you would normally shift but also tolerates short-shifting like a 450.
On the 2021 bike map 1 is broad and easy with plenty of over-rev; map 2 pulls harder low and in the middle but goes flat sooner on top.
In deep sand or whooped, cupped tracks the stock setup rides deep and pitches, so riders add compression and adjust air and sag.
Stock throttle cam has a very long throw; testers fit the quick-turn cam supplied with the bike.
Neutral is hard to find when stopped.
2022 bikes: starter wire pulling out of its junction box, FI light falling out, preload ring chipping, bar mounts twisting and rear brake springs breaking.
Some owners hear a loud top-end rattle for a few seconds after a cold start or hot restart, usually blamed on the hydraulic cam-chain tensioner.

common_fixes.problem: Rides deep and pitches in sand and whoops
common_fixes.fix: Stiffer compression and more fork air; 103-110 mm sag in deep sand
common_fixes.result: Better hold-up and less air-fork harshness in soft terrain

common_fixes.fix: Fit the supplied quick-turn throttle cam
common_fixes.result: Quicker throttle and less arm pump

common_fixes.fix: High-speed compression in 1/4 turn
common_fixes.result: Fewer G-out bottoming hits

bikes.summary: Testers agree the current 350 SX-F picks up quickly, pulls harder through the middle than the old bike and makes its best power at the top, so it wants to be revved out. They describe it as pulling like a 450 out of corners while revving like a 250, less tiring than a 450 but weaker on long starts. The 2023-2024 chassis is stiff and harsh until broken in, the shock lacks end-stroke support for fast riders, and the 2025 frame is more comfortable. Common changes are the aggressive map, an extra rear sprocket tooth, an aftermarket ECU or remap, a linkage, and chain slack near 70 mm.

points.statement: Picks up quickly off the bottom, pulls harder through the middle than the 2019-2022 engine and is strongest at the top, so it should be revved to the limiter.
Pulls like a 450 out of corners and revs like a 250, but has less low-end grunt than a 450 and cannot pull tall gears the same way.
Feels lighter and less tiring than a 450 even though claimed weights are almost the same, mainly due to softer delivery and less rotating mass.
Starts are weaker than a 450 on long start straights.
Peak power is a few hp short of most 450s and arrives well over 11,000 rpm, roughly 1,400-2,400 rpm higher than a 450.
Most testers race the aggressive map 2 for a snappier, more 450-like feel; the standard map suits novices, vets and slick hard pack.
Quickshifter can feel boggy at half throttle or on jump faces, so testers often turn it off.
Traction control watches for runaway rpm, so it helps only in mud, rain or rock-hard slick dirt.
The 2023-2024 frame is stiffer and heavier, feels harsh until about 10 hours of break-in, but is stable under braking.
The 2025 frame is more comfortable and compliant than 2024 with the same geometry.
Fast riders find the shock lacks end-stroke support and bottoms harshly.
Many testers add a rear sprocket tooth (some two) for more low-to-mid thrust or to use third in corners.
Needs about 68-70 mm of chain slack; too little chews the swingarm buffer and loads the suspension.
Swingarm pivot nut can back out from vibration; check it or use thread locker.
Spokes near the rear rim lock loosen; small plastic radiator cap can loosen or be hard to open (threaded cap from 2026); neutral hard to find on the line.
Many owners report decel popping and some report low-rpm stalling in slow sections.

common_fixes.problem: Wants more low-end snap and clean decel
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket ECU mapped for the exhaust and fuel, or a stock-ECU remap where available
common_fixes.result: Crisper response, stronger mid and over-rev, less popping and engine braking

common_fixes.problem: Shock bottoms at end of stroke
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket linkage, stiffer bumpers or more low-speed compression
common_fixes.result: Better end-stroke support

common_fixes.fix: Swingarm pivot bolt at 95 Nm (thread-locked)
common_fixes.result: Rear settles and tracks straighter

common_fixes.problem: Nervous at speed / vague in ruts
common_fixes.fix: 23.5 mm offset clamps
common_fixes.result: Calmer straight-line and better front feel in ruts

common_fixes.fix: Full titanium exhaust
common_fixes.result: More mid-rpm response and pull with stock-like over-rev, about 2 lb lighter

common_fixes.fix: Vented airbox cover
common_fixes.result: Better low-to-mid response

common_fixes.fix: Raise TPS voltage slightly, check header seals, or remap
common_fixes.result: Reported to reduce popping (no confirmed root cause)

sides: Snappier off the bottom
Smoother off the bottom with less engine braking
Peaks later rather than harder
Aftermarket ECU worth it for extra maps and response
A cheap remap of the stock ECU gets most of the benefit

bikes.summary: Testers describe the previous FC 350 as smooth, linear and sneaky fast with a big over-rev, broad and easy to modulate rather than torquey. The stock air fork needed attention: one tester found it soft and divey on decel, another short on initial comfort, and pressure had to be checked every ride. The lowered 2021-2022 chassis was rated a top handler. Intake screen removal, fork air changes and a stiffer shock spring for heavier riders are typical changes.

points.statement: Smooth, linear and broad off the bottom with a big over-rev; easy to modulate and faster than it feels.
Nearly matches a 450's top speed on the flat but loses out uphill; recovers better than a 450 when in the wrong gear.
Noticeable engine braking in second gear, much less in third.
Stock air fork needs attention: soft and divey on decel for one tester, short on initial comfort for another, with pressure checks needed every ride.
Shock empties at the end of the stroke on G-outs and jump faces.
The lowered 2021-2022 chassis was rated best-handling, with a low centre of gravity and easy ground reach.
2022 composite subframe cracked at the lower right bolt hole.
Stock seat cover too grippy and bar low when standing.

common_fixes.problem: Fork soft and divey on decel
common_fixes.fix: Add air (about 10.8 bar)
common_fixes.result: More hold-up and comfort

common_fixes.problem: Air fork lacks comfort and consistency
common_fixes.fix: Coil conversion using KYB internals in the WP tubes
common_fixes.result: More comfort, better front contact and bottoming control

common_fixes.fix: High-speed compression in 1/8-1/4 turn
common_fixes.result: Balanced the bike

common_fixes.fix: Cut out the backfire screen or fit a two-stroke filter cage
common_fixes.result: Runs more like the KTM

common_fixes.problem: Shock spring soft for a 190 lb rider
common_fixes.fix: Go up to 45 N/mm (or 48)
common_fixes.result: Suggested by owners; no tested outcome reported

disagreements.topic: Magura clutch feel versus the KTM's Brembo
sides: Magura is smoother
Magura is more on/off

bikes.generation: 2023+ generation (lowered KTM platform; no 2026 US model)
bikes.summary: The current FC 350 shares the KTM engine and frame but sits lower, and testers rate it best of the three brands for handling, comfort and reaching the ground. Its closed airbox mutes low-end response compared with the KTM. The 2023 frame felt stiff and harsh until broken in, and on hard pack testers mostly reduced compression damping. Tuners note its valving differs from the KTM, so KTM settings do not carry over.

points.statement: Lower chassis gives the best handling and comfort of the three brands and makes it easy to touch the ground.
Muted low-end response compared with the barkier KTM.
2023 frame is stiff and feels harsh until broken in; testers soften the fork to compensate.
On hard pack most testers reduced compression at both ends and tuned with clickers rather than air.
Testers often turn the quickshifter off.
One owner reported rich blubbering at quarter throttle and repeated stalling in a harescramble.

common_fixes.fix: Check crankcase breather hose routing (often pinched after linkage service)
common_fixes.result: Clutch works normally again

sides: Peaks later rather than harder
Snappier off the bottom

bikes.summary: Few tester findings exist for the first-generation MC 350F. Testers found it lively low with a long rev, smoother off the bottom than the KTM 350 but harder than the Husqvarna, and lighter than both on the 2023 scale. It ran only the mellow map without an accessory switch.

points.statement: Lively low and revs long; smoother off the bottom than the KTM 350 but harder-hitting than the FC 350.
On the old platform it weighed about 5-6 lb less than the KTM or Husqvarna 350.
Only the mellow map without an accessory switch; no quickshift, traction or launch control.
Testers turned shock high-speed compression in a quarter turn to reduce G-out bottoming and ran more rebound than recommended.

bikes.summary: The current MC 350F shares the KTM engine, frame and wheels but uses forged clamps, softer damping, taller bars and Braktec brakes, and ships with only the mellow map. Testers find its low-end response muted by intake and exhaust restrictions, and its softer suspension suits hard pack and slower riders. Brake opinions split: some find the Braktec units strong, others say they lack modulation.

points.statement: Intake and exhaust restrictions (no resonance chamber, muffler restrictor, small airbox vent) mute low-end response compared with the KTM.
Second gear is punchy but it revs out and cannot pull third or fourth like a 450.
Softer valving than the KTM; it works on hard pack and for slower riders.
On slick hard pack one tester preferred the mellow map; the aggressive map had more punch low but less mid torque.
2024 chassis changes direction and cuts under ruts easily.

common_fixes.fix: Accessory map switch (about $170-180)
common_fixes.result: Unlocks the aggressive map, traction control, launch control and quickshifter

common_fixes.fix: One tooth smaller rear sprocket (51)
common_fixes.result: Less abrupt second gear

common_fixes.fix: Drill or replace the airbox cover; slip-on or KTM stock pipe
common_fixes.result: Sharper response; peak power reportedly unaffected

sides: Strong, no fade, as good as Brembo
Less modulation than Brembo

bikes.summary: Testers describe the previous 250 SX-F as soft below about 6,000 rpm and then pulling harder and harder to a very high peak with long over-rev, rewarding riders who keep it revving. Stock gearing feels tall, so testers commonly go to a 13-tooth countershaft or add rear teeth. The air fork needs several hours to break in. Hardware such as the counterbalancer needle bearing and various bolts needed watching.

points.statement: Soft below about 6,000 rpm, then pulls harder to a peak near 13,400-13,900 rpm with long over-rev; it rewards aggressive riders and punishes lazy shifting.
Stock 14/51 gearing feels tall and sluggish out of tight turns, especially for slower or heavier riders.
Air fork needs about 5-6 engine hours to break in; extra air helped hold-up on decel.
Counterbalancer needle bearing could walk out (changed to a bushing for 2022); sprocket, head-stay and subframe bolts and the linkage nut could loosen.

common_fixes.fix: 13-tooth countershaft or 14/52-14/53
common_fixes.result: Better corner-exit surge and more use of third

common_fixes.fix: Vented airbox cover
common_fixes.result: Filled the dip with almost no change at peak

common_fixes.fix: Stiffer low-speed compression; 1/4 turn more high-speed if still soft at end of stroke
common_fixes.result: Less squat and better end-stroke control

bikes.generation: 2023+ generation (81 x 48.5 mm engine, new frame)
bikes.summary: Testers consistently describe the current 250 SX-F engine as quiet and very linear: less exciting off the bottom than a Yamaha or Honda, but with a strong midrange and a top end that keeps pulling after rivals sign off, giving the widest usable power window in the class. It wins or places second in most 250 shootouts. The air fork and the new frame feel stiff until broken in, and the fork's pressure drift means checks before every ride. Testers race the aggressive map with traction control off, fit the vented airbox cover and keep chain slack near 65-70 mm.

points.statement: Quiet, very linear engine with a strong midrange that does its best work above about 11,000 rpm and keeps pulling after rivals sign off, giving the widest usable power window in the class.
Bottom end feels less exciting than a Yamaha or Honda; it needs revs and a big throttle opening to show its speed, so it feels slower than the dyno says.
Wins or places second in 250 four-stroke shootouts.
About 6 lb heavier than the 2022 bike on the scale.
Most testers race the aggressive map; the mellow map suits very light riders, novices or slick tracks.
On 2023-2024 bikes traction control cut power by roughly a quarter and made the engine run rough, so testers leave it off; the 2025 update made it usable on wet or very hard tracks.
Air fork pressure rises in the sun and while riding, so it must be set cold and bled before each ride; drift hurts consistency.
Fork and frame feel stiff and harsh when new; testers allow about 6-10 hours of break-in before judging.
Frame squats less under power, pitches less under braking and is very stable; the 2025 frame reduced harshness in acceleration chop.
The stock 42 N/mm shock spring suits riders up to about 175-180 lb; heavier riders go to 45 N/mm.
2023 shock is not firm enough at the very end of its stroke; more low-speed compression controls it.
Linkage needle bearings can walk out and bind; spokes by the rear rim lock loosen during break-in; plastic radiator cap is hard to remove and has leaked.
Chain should run 65-70 mm slack at the buffer pad, which looks loose; tighter chains wear the buffer quickly.
A few owners report 2023 bikes turning hard to start cold, blamed on a stuck ring or tightening valves; a leak-down test is advised.

common_fixes.fix: Vented airbox cover
common_fixes.result: Sharper response; on the older engine it filled a midrange dip

common_fixes.problem: Rider will not rev the engine
common_fixes.fix: One more tooth on the rear sprocket
common_fixes.result: More low-rpm pull

common_fixes.fix: Coil cartridge conversion
common_fixes.result: Better hand comfort and ground-following with no pressure checks

common_fixes.fix: Caged linkage bearing 58033097000
common_fixes.result: Linkage moves freely

common_fixes.fix: Run 65-70 mm slack; aftermarket buffer pad
common_fixes.result: Buffer lasts; 2025 raised the pad from the factory

sides: Slightly less snappy off the bottom
Noticeably punchier off the bottom
Character largely unchanged
First in class
Second behind the YZ250F

bikes.summary: Testers describe the previous FC 250 as smooth and linear, mellow at the bottom and very fast when revved, and less snappy than the KTM because of its more restrictive airbox. Its stock gearing feels tall, the 2020 suspension settings came out too soft for most riders, and a light rider found the fork harsh on small chatter. A recurring list of KTM-family maintenance items applies, and the rear brake pedal spring breaks often.

points.statement: Smooth and linear off the bottom, building to a big over-rev; easier and less snappy than the KTM and can be ridden a gear high.
Restrictive airbox makes it smoother and less aggressive than the KTM, even in the aggressive map.
Stock 14/51 feels sluggish; at least one more rear tooth or a 13-tooth countershaft is needed.
2020 settings came out too soft for most buyers; one light rider found the 2021 fork harsh on low-speed chatter.
Rear brake pedal spring breaks every 4-5 hours; throttle cables wear around 20 hours; spokes, engine-hanger and pivot bolts back out.
Header sticks out and burns pants; stock bar low for a 6 ft rider.
Recommended over a 450 for most vets and weekend riders, even older ones.

common_fixes.fix: Screenless two-stroke filter cage, cutting the backfire screen, or drilling the vented cover
common_fixes.result: Cheapest gain; runs more like the KTM

common_fixes.problem: Low-speed chatter harsh for a light rider
common_fixes.fix: Drop fork air to about 10.2 bar
common_fixes.result: Fixed without bottoming

common_fixes.problem: Fork soft and divey on decel
common_fixes.fix: Add air (about 10.7 bar)
common_fixes.result: More hold-up and comfort

common_fixes.fix: Honda CRF450R spring or aftermarket return spring
common_fixes.result: Spring stops breaking

common_fixes.problem: Fixed left axle block stiffens rear on throttle
common_fixes.fix: Floating axle blocks
common_fixes.result: More rear compliance

disagreements.topic: FC 250 power versus the identical KTM
sides: Regularly out-dynos the KTM
Matches the KTM and falls behind above about 12,700 rpm

disagreements.topic: Magura clutch feel versus the KTM's Brembo
sides: Magura is smoother
Magura is more on/off

bikes.summary: The current FC 250 uses the KTM engine, and on the dyno it matches the KTM, but its tightly closed airbox makes it softer and smoother off the bottom on the track; once on the pipe it pulls hard and wants to be revved. It sits about an inch lower, turns tighter and suits shorter, lighter and novice-to-vet riders, and testers set it up a bit stiffer than the KTM. The 2025 frame is calmer in acceleration chop and breaks in sooner. Shootout results range from second to fifth.

points.statement: Same engine as the KTM, but the closed airbox makes it softer and smoother off the bottom; it pulls hard from the middle and wants high revs.
Dyno numbers are essentially the same as the KTM's.
Sits about an inch lower and turns tighter; suits shorter, lighter and novice-to-vet riders.
Testers set it up stiffer than the KTM: one found the stock valving too soft for serious racing, another runs firmer settings because it sits lower.
The 2025 frame is calmer, more comfortable leaned over and less jarring on acceleration bumps, and settles sooner in break-in.
Initial harshness when new, typical of the Austrian bikes, settled after a few days.
Quickshifter works well and the Brembo clutch is very durable.
On 2023-2024 bikes traction control cut power heavily and was nearly unusable.
Linkage needle bearings can walk out and make the rear feel dead.

common_fixes.fix: Perforated alternative airbox panel or vented cover
common_fixes.result: Sharper throttle response

common_fixes.problem: Default connectivity-unit setting felt jerky with too much engine braking
common_fixes.fix: Engine braking 1/5, aggressive output, response 4/5
common_fixes.result: Freer engine and calmer chassis

common_fixes.problem: Wants more front-end steering and grip
common_fixes.fix: Open shock high-speed compression to 1.75 turns out
common_fixes.result: More front bite in corners

common_fixes.problem: Shock speeds up at end of stroke
common_fixes.fix: More low-speed compression
common_fixes.result: Controlled end-stroke drop

sides: Second in class three years running
Fifth, marked down for its lowered chassis and price
Aggressive map 2 preferred
Map 1 on track, map 2 with traction control for rocky single track

bikes.summary: Only one early first ride exists. Testers called it the easiest bike in the range, with good low-end torque, smooth non-aggressive power and soft suspension that stays calm at slower speeds.

points.statement: Good low-end torque; pulls out of corners even a gear too high with smooth, non-aggressive power.
Soft suspension stays calm over bumps at slower speeds.

bikes.summary: The first MC 250F is the KTM 250 SX-F with a near-sealed airbox, plain header, muffler restrictors, forged clamps, softer valving and no map switch. Testers found a soft low end with a clear dip before strong mid-to-top pull, and stock gearing that feels tall. In 2023, still on the old platform, it was the lightest bike in its class.

points.statement: Soft low-rpm response with a clear dip from about 3,500 to 6,000 rpm, then strong from the middle to the top.
Stock 14/51 feels sluggish out of corners.
On the old platform in 2023 it was the lightest 250F in its class.
Felt pitchy with weight transfer until setup changes; some testers liked up to 108 mm sag.
Forged clamps flex more than billet clamps, giving vague turn-in.
No map switch: map 1 only until an accessory switch is fitted.

common_fixes.fix: Cut the airbox winglet or fit a KTM vented cover
common_fixes.result: Better breathing and response

common_fixes.fix: 13-tooth countershaft (13/50) or 14/52
common_fixes.result: Better corner-exit surge

bikes.summary: On the current KTM platform the MC 250F measures essentially the same as the KTM on the dyno, but its closed airbox, muffler restrictor and single stock map dull throttle response on the track; testers disagree on whether that makes it fun or held back. Softer valving makes it comfortable for vets and novices on soft tracks but short on hold-up for fast riders on jumpy tracks. Braktec brakes and clutch are rated below the Brembo parts, and it finishes mid-pack in shootouts.

points.statement: Dyno numbers are close to the KTM and Husqvarna (within about 1-2 hp), and in some tests slightly ahead.
Closed airbox, muffler restrictor and single stock map dull throttle response on the track more than the dyno shows.
2024 engine has better bottom torque than the previous one and revs a long way.
Softer valving than the KTM: comfortable with easy traction on soft or rough tracks for vets and novices, but less hold-up for fast riders on jumpy tracks.
Air fork is sensitive: a 5 psi change is clearly felt.
2025 frame cut-outs make it more comfortable in acceleration chop.
Braktec brakes stop well but with less precise modulation than Brembo; front brake subject to recall.
Braktec clutch feel changes when fanned or held at high rpm, causing a surge.
Right radiator wing blocks the fork compression clickers; bars are 12 mm taller than the KTM's.
One-piece airbox side panel fits loosely and can be knocked off by a boot.
Stock Maxxis tires lack side-knob grip.
Finishes mid-pack in shootouts, behind the KTM and Husqvarna.

common_fixes.problem: Restricted intake, exhaust and single map
common_fixes.fix: Accessory map switch, drilled or swapped airbox cover, unrestricted muffler
common_fixes.result: Brings it close to KTM feel (no dyno before/after published)

common_fixes.fix: Run 65-70 mm chain slack at the buffer pad
common_fixes.result: Chassis works best at that slack

sides: Held back by intake and exhaust restrictions
Most fun of the three Austrian engines
Strong with no fade
Less precise modulation than Brembo

bikes.summary: The carbureted 125 SX won one magazine's 125 shootouts in 2021 and 2022, ahead of its Husqvarna and GasGas siblings and the YZ125. Little else is reported beyond the usual KTM-family checks and owner jetting reports that lean toward the lean side.

points.statement: Won 125 two-stroke shootouts in 2021 and 2022, ahead of the Husqvarna, GasGas and YZ125.
Spokes by the rim lock loosen during break-in and the rear brake pedal spring can fall off or break.
Owners report some jetting combinations running lean and hot; use owner settings only as a direction.

common_fixes.fix: Drop fork air 0.2-0.5 bar to rebalance
common_fixes.result: Keeps front and rear in balance

common_fixes.fix: Vented airbox cover or drilled cover, then re-check jetting
common_fixes.result: More bottom-end power and response

bikes.summary: Testers find the TBI 125 SX a little slower off the crack than the carbureted bike but easier to keep on the pipe, with smoother delivery that helps traction and suits novices more than top racers; the old carb bike keeps pulling higher on top. One magazine had repeated detonation on pump fuel, worse with an aftermarket pipe, and found the green map bogged randomly, while another tester saw no detonation. The ECU was locked at launch.

points.statement: Slightly slower off the crack than the carb 125 but rolls into the power more easily and stays on the pipe with less effort; tapers on top where the carb bike keeps climbing.
Detonated repeatedly on pump fuel in testing, worse with an aftermarket pipe; the 2024 model got no mapping fix.
The richer green map bogged at random on test bikes, so testers used the white map.
Stock ECU was locked at launch with no aftermarket ECU available.
2024 valving changes could not be felt on track; the suspension gets plusher after break-in.
A dealer reported 2025 bikes that would not start or fouled plugs; cycling the fuel pump, waiting for the light to go out and fresh correctly mixed fuel fixed them.

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe (one brand gave more low-mid and less clutch use; another the snappiest bottom and longest over-rev)
common_fixes.result: Closer to 150 feel

common_fixes.fix: Remap needed with an aftermarket pipe
common_fixes.result: Testers say a pipe alone made detonation worse

sides: Repeated detonation on pump fuel, worse with a pipe
No detonation seen with aftermarket pipes

bikes.summary: The carbureted 150 SX makes about 3 hp more than the 125 but hits hard in the middle and signs off quickly, so testers find the 125 smoother. Holding a gear too long unsettles the chassis. Findings come from one magazine.

points.statement: About 3 hp more than the 125, but hits hard in the midrange and signs off fast; the 125 feels smoother.
Holding a gear too long shifts weight forward and unsettles the chassis.
Fast riders preferred 14/49 over stock 13/48; tight tracks or less skilled riders 14/50.

common_fixes.fix: Stamped aftermarket pipe
common_fixes.result: About 2 hp more at peak, smoother mid so third is usable, quicker rev

bikes.summary: One reviewer found the stock TBI 150 SX dull at the bottom, strongest in the midrange and fading on top, so riders short-shifted; an aftermarket pipe and silencer fixed most of that. A dealer also reported no-start and plug-fouling cases on 2025 bikes.

points.statement: Stock engine is dull at the bottom, strongest in the midrange and fades on top, so riders short-shift.
Some 2025 bikes would not start or fouled plugs until the fuel pump was cycled and fresh, correctly mixed fuel used.

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe and silencer
common_fixes.result: Better bottom response, slightly more mid and a much longer over-rev

bikes.summary: In one magazine's 125 shootouts the carbureted TC 125 handled best of the group, but its composite airbox muted throttle response enough to cost pro testers lap time. Stock shock settings were close, and the fork is sensitive to height in the clamps.

points.statement: Handled best in the 125 shootout.
Composite airbox mutes throttle response; pro testers were up to 2 seconds a lap slower than on the KTM.
Fork is sensitive to clamp height; stock shock settings were close after setting sag.

bikes.summary: The TBI TC 125 sits lower than the KTM with softer fork action. Like the KTM it detonated on pump fuel in testing, worse with a pipe, and its green map bogged; the ECU was locked at launch.

points.statement: Forks 10 mm shorter and changed linkage lower the seat, with softer fork action than the KTM.
Detonation on pump fuel, made worse by an aftermarket pipe even on race fuel.
Green map bogged at random; ECU locked at launch.

common_fixes.fix: Remap the ECU
common_fixes.result: Needed before a pipe can be run safely

bikes.summary: Only dyno and technical reporting exist. The bigger bore gives about 3 hp more than a 125 on the same dyno, and the lowered chassis and closed-off subframe follow the Husqvarna pattern.

points.statement: Made about 3 hp and 1 lb-ft more than a 125 SX on the same dyno.
Rear of the subframe is closed off, cutting airflow to the engine compared with the KTM.

bikes.summary: The carbureted MC 125 uses the KTM engine with a closed airbox, forged clamps and softer suspension. Testers found a strong midrange and good top-end pull blunted at the first crack of throttle by the airbox, plusher suspension aimed at novices and vets, and clamps that flex enough to affect steering. In 2023 it out-revved the new TBI KTM and Husqvarna on top.

points.statement: Same WP hardware as the KTM with softer valving, plusher and aimed at novice and vet riders.
A 200 lb rider would need a stiffer shock spring.
Closed airbox cover blunts initial throttle response.
Strong midrange and good top-end pull; in 2023 it kept climbing on top where the TBI siblings tapered.
Forged clamps flex more than billet ones, causing oversteer on entry and understeer on exit.
One 160 lb owner found the manual's lower air pressure felt great after higher pressure felt soft at speed and pogo-like slow.

common_fixes.fix: Vented aftermarket cover or drilled stock cover
common_fixes.result: Sharper first crack of throttle

bikes.summary: Testers found the TBI MC 125 smoother and more predictable than the carbureted bike, with power shifted toward the midrange and fewer peaks and dips after a missed shift.

points.statement: Power shifted toward the midrange; more predictable and four-stroke-like with fewer peaks and dips after a missed shift.

bikes.summary: Testers found the carbureted 250 SX strongest from bottom to mid with an aggressive hit, then little top end, and less explosive than the 2017-2018 bike mainly because of airbox restriction. It out-pulled the YZ250 low and in the middle on the dyno. Stock fork settings felt stiff, and some owners still prefer it to the heavier TBI model.

points.statement: Strongest bottom to mid with an aggressive hit, then little top end; it out-pulls the YZ250 to about 8,800 rpm and then falls off.
Stock fork felt stiff and harsh until broken in; testers lowered air and opened compression significantly.
Owners say the TBI 250 that replaced it makes less power and weighs more.
Shock preload ring wears quickly; there is no oil sight glass so oil is checked at a weep bolt.

common_fixes.fix: Optional vented airbox cover or drilled cover, then re-jet
common_fixes.result: More bottom-end power and response

common_fixes.fix: One tooth smaller rear sprocket
common_fixes.result: Calmer bottom and spread gears

bikes.summary: Testers agree the TBI 250 SX's stock mapping is conservative: a luggable, almost four-stroke-like bottom end, then a flat top that runs into an abrupt limiter. Remaps and aftermarket pipes are the standard fix and add mid-to-top pull. Stock suspension is balanced on hard tracks but soft for heavier or faster riders. A few owners reported brief cut-outs on 2023 bikes.

points.statement: Stock mapping is conservative: luggable bottom end but flat on top and quick to reach the rev limiter.
Revs through the gears quicker than the 300.
The white map opens the power valve only about 80% and mutes power; the green map opens it fully.
Rev limiter is abrupt, mostly when revving with the clutch in or in the air.
Stock suspension is balanced on hard West Coast tracks but soft for heavier or faster riders and for deep loam or sand.
A few 2023 owners reported brief cut-outs under load or in the air; dealers could not reproduce them.

common_fixes.problem: Flat top end and limiter hits
common_fixes.fix: Remap of the stock ECU
common_fixes.result: Keeps the luggable bottom while adding mid-to-top pull and fewer limiter hits

common_fixes.problem: Rich low-rpm feel and flat top
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe and silencer
common_fixes.result: Cleaner low end, more second-gear pull and much stronger top end

bikes.summary: Testers like the TBI 300 SX's strong, luggable low-to-mid torque, which lets riders hold second or third with fewer shifts, but the stock mapping has a short over-rev and runs flat on top. The white map is mellower with a longer pull, the green map hits harder. Stock suspension is soft for riders over about 185 lb, though one east-coast tester found it firm. Aftermarket pipes are the most-tested fix and add measurable power; a remap adds over-rev.

points.statement: Strong, luggable low-to-mid torque lets riders hold second or third with fewer shifts.
Stock delivery has a short midrange ramp and short over-rev, so it needs quick shifts or runs flat at high rpm.
White map is mellower with a longer pull; green map hits harder and needs more clutch work.
Stock suspension gets soft for riders over about 185 lb.
Owners report water in the throttle-position-sensor connector causing fouled plugs and cut-outs, and re-teach the electronic power valve periodically.

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe and silencer
common_fixes.result: Measured about 3 hp more on one dyno; more mid, snap and over-rev, third usable in corners

common_fixes.fix: ECU remap
common_fixes.result: More traditional hit, more over-rev and better third-gear exits

common_fixes.problem: Weak third-gear roll-on in loose dirt
common_fixes.fix: One more rear tooth (13/50)
common_fixes.result: Better third-gear pull

common_fixes.fix: One step hotter spark plug
common_fixes.result: Used by one tester to cure detonation

sides: Soft over about 185 lb
Firm; changes made it smoother and plusher

bikes.summary: Findings come from one magazine. The carbureted TC 250 breathes through a composite airbox that gives softer throttle response than the KTM, its power is concentrated bottom to mid so it needs more shifting, and it sits about an inch lower with softer valving. Stock suspension settings felt stiff to vet testers.

points.statement: Composite subframe and airbox breathe less than the KTM's, softening throttle response.
Power is concentrated bottom to mid and needs more shifting than a YZ250.
Stock settings felt stiff; vet testers lowered air and opened compression.
Handlebar map switch is hidden under the throttle cables and hard to read.

common_fixes.fix: Vent the airbox cover (large holes away from the filter), re-check jetting
common_fixes.result: More throttle snap; fast testers liked it, slow ones did not

bikes.summary: The TBI TC 250 sits about an inch lower than the KTM with a closed airbox that dulls the first crack of throttle and softer valving aimed at novices and vets; faster riders wanted more support. An aftermarket pipe filled a dip in its curve. One owner traced a mid-ride cut-out to a failed fuel pump.

points.statement: Closed airbox slightly dulls the first crack of throttle.
Softer valving with less hold-up than the KTM 300 SX: better traction and fit for shorter riders, less support for fast riders.
One owner's bike lost power and died about 15 minutes into rides; the fuel pump was faulty.

common_fixes.problem: Dip in the curve at 7,600-8,000 rpm
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe and silencer
common_fixes.result: About 1 hp more at peak and the dip removed

common_fixes.fix: Forks flush, high-speed compression 1 turn out
common_fixes.result: More hold-up

bikes.summary: Only owner reports exist: smooth, linear and luggable, smoother than a YZ250, but some feel it runs out of steam early in stock form and recommend a remap.

points.statement: Smooth, linear and luggable; some owners feel it runs out of steam early stock.

common_fixes.fix: ECU remap, often with a 49-tooth sprocket
common_fixes.result: More over-rev

bikes.summary: Findings come from one magazine. The carbureted MC 250 hits hard from the bottom and pulls hard into the middle but signs off early, so it needs short-shifting; taller gearing calms it. Suspension is softer and suited to novices and vets, and the forged clamps flex.

points.statement: Hits hard from the bottom and pulls harder into the middle than a YZ250 but signs off early, so it needs short-shifting.
Softer settings suit novice and vet riders; fast or heavy riders go stiffer or to a 45 N/mm spring.
Forged clamps flex more than billet ones.
In 2023 it was about 7 lb lighter and $600 cheaper than the TBI KTM.

common_fixes.fix: One tooth taller gearing (14/48)
common_fixes.result: Calmer bottom and better gear spacing

bikes.summary: Testers found the TBI MC 250 crisp and clean with very strong low-end torque that pulls third in slow sections. One launch tester found the anti-squat rear odd at first but good for driving out of corners, and the air fork harsh on small high-speed bumps. The map switch was an option on the tested bike and was the first suggested upgrade.

points.statement: Crisp, clean delivery with very strong low-end torque that pulls third gear in slow sections.
Anti-squat rear feels odd at first on corner exits but lets the rider get on the throttle harder; shock is forgiving.
Air fork handles big landings but feels harsh on small high-speed bumps.
Map switch was optional on the test bike; standard map for hard pack, green map for sand.

common_fixes.problem: Fork too stiff for a 74 kg rider
common_fixes.fix: 140-145 psi; sag raised to about 103 mm
common_fixes.result: Sharper steering, at some cost to downhill stability

bikes.summary: Testers describe the 2018-2024 85 SX as having little bottom end before exploding into its midrange. Small complaints include a soft plastic shock preload ring, a power-valve adjuster that needs a square-drive wrench and a hard-to-remove airbox cover. Parents report the air fork can feel harsh on landings for very light riders.

points.statement: Little bottom end, then explodes into the midrange; later testers called it lazy off the bottom.
Soft plastic shock preload ring, square-drive power-valve adjuster, Torx fork bleed screw and a hard-to-remove airbox cover.
Parents report the air fork can feel harsh on landings for light riders; one never got it right until a coil conversion.

common_fixes.problem: Harsh fork for a light rider
common_fixes.fix: Open compression rather than dropping air; coil conversion as last resort
common_fixes.result: Owner-reported improvements

bikes.summary: Testers found the 2025 KTM-group 85 stronger off the bottom than the 2024 bike, smooth into the midrange and still snappy on top, and most testers picked it as the best 85. Complaints: rich stock jetting, brittle plastics, hidden shock clickers, weaker Formula brakes and low bars.

points.statement: Pulls harder off the bottom than the 2024 bike, transitions smoothly into the midrange and keeps its top-end snap; picked as best 85 by most testers.
Stock jetting runs rich, leaving oil residue and a slight midrange flat spot.
Rigid plastic fenders snap in small crashes.
Formula brakes are weaker than the Brembos on the big bikes.
Testers wanted taller bars; side panels hide the shock clickers; steering lock is tight.

common_fixes.fix: Lean the pilot (42-52) and adjust main/needle as advised
common_fixes.result: Cleaned up the rich midrange

common_fixes.fix: Drill an access hole in the side panel
common_fixes.result: Clickers reachable without removing plastics

bikes.summary: Tested as the same bike as the 2025 KTM 85 SX: stronger and smoother off the bottom than the 2024 version, with rich stock jetting and brittle plastics.

points.statement: Pulls harder off the bottom than the 2024 bike and transitions smoothly into the midrange while keeping its top-end snap.
Stock jetting runs rich with a slight midrange flat spot.
Rigid plastic fenders snap in crashes; air fork needs a pressure check before every ride.

common_fixes.fix: Pilot dropped to 42 with an NRJC needle in the third clip (advised by factory R&D)
common_fixes.result: Cleaned up the midrange

bikes.summary: In one 85 comparison the Husqvarna version, with its closed airbox, pulled shorter and ran richer than the KTM and GasGas versions.

points.statement: Closed airbox makes it pull less far on top and run richer than the KTM and GasGas versions.

bikes.summary: Testers describe the previous 450 XC-F as an SX-F engine with mellower cross-country mapping: soft off the bottom, smooth and strong once going, and it hooks up well. Its five-speed gearbox is the main complaint, with first too tall for tight trails and too few gears for fast desert, so a sixth gear is a popular swap. Suspension is plush on trail chatter but lacks the SX-F's hold-up on jumps, and it shipped without a skid plate or spark arrester.

points.statement: Mellow off the bottom, smooth and surge-free through the middle and strong once going; hooks up with less wheelspin and feels slower than it is.
Five-speed gearbox: first is too tall for tight trails and it runs out of gear in fast desert.
Softer cross-country valving is plush on trail chatter but lacks the SX-F's hold-up on jumps.
Shipped without a skid plate, engine protection or a USFS spark arrester despite costing more than the SX-F.

common_fixes.problem: Runs out of gear in the desert
common_fixes.fix: Add the OEM sixth-gear pair and shift drum (about $300, cases split), often with 14/48 sprockets
common_fixes.result: Usable top gear for fast terrain

common_fixes.problem: Not enough hold-up for GP racing
common_fixes.fix: Fork air raised 0.5 bar and shock high-speed compression in 1/4 turn
common_fixes.result: Stronger hold-up (0.5 bar is a big change)

bikes.summary: Testers find the current 450 XC-F as powerful as any production 450 yet manageable and linear, but more prone than a 350 or XC-W to stalling and flame-outs in slow technical terrain. The 2023-2024 frame felt too rigid and the 2025 frame is more compliant. Its soft cross-country suspension suits WORCS and hare scrambles, while the 2026 coil fork rides low and bottoms on fast ground. Desert racers add a sixth gear to the five-speed.

points.statement: As much peak power as any production 450, yet linear and manageable, pulling cleanly from off idle and revving far.
Stalls and flames out more easily than a 350 or XC-W in tight, slow terrain; the spinning mass makes low-speed work harder.
The 2023-2024 frame felt too rigid; the 2025 frame is more compliant almost everywhere.
Shock is valved like a soft motocross setting: good for WORCS-style racing but too stiff in desert rock fields; fork slightly stiff picking through boulders.
The 2026 coil fork rides low and softer than the rear, giving a nose-down feel and bottoming in fast terrain; suits hare scrambles and some prefer the old air fork.
The five-speed runs out of gear on fast desert; many racers add a sixth gear.
Clutch-heavy riders can overheat the clutch in tight single track.

common_fixes.problem: Runs out of gear in the desert
common_fixes.fix: Fit a sixth gear
common_fixes.result: Top gear for fast terrain

common_fixes.fix: Firmer settings for speed or revalve for rocks
common_fixes.result: Desert racers need different settings from WORCS racers

bikes.summary: Testers like the current 350 XC-F's strong bottom-end pull, good midrange and extra pull on top, rideable like a 450 but rewarding revs. Its weak spots are jerky low-speed throttle response and stalling in tight rocky terrain, a coil fork that is softer than the shock and pitches or blows through, and a clutch that overheats or fades under heavy slipping. Testers try shorter gearing with mixed results.

points.statement: Strong bottom-end pull, good midrange and more pull on top; can be ridden like a 450 but rewards revving.
Low-speed throttle response is jerky in slow rocky sections and it can cough and stall in tight single track.
Coil fork is softer than the shock: it pitches under hard braking and blows through on big hits, and is soft for aggressive motocross.
Heavy clutch use in tight single track overheats or fades the clutch; one tester boiled coolant twice.
The 2023 air fork worked at stock settings for desert and motocross after break-in but was harsh before 6-8 hours.
Testers try shorter gearing to use third in corners; results are mixed (one went back to stock because second became too short).

common_fixes.problem: Stalling and coughing in tight terrain
common_fixes.fix: Turn traction control off on the soft map; shorter header, aftermarket silencer and custom map
common_fixes.result: Cleaner running and less stalling

common_fixes.fix: Auto-clutch, lower gearing, smoother map, or the 450 SX-F clutch master cylinder
common_fixes.result: Less fade and heat

common_fixes.problem: Soft fork pitches and blows through
common_fixes.fix: Revalve and springs for rider weight, about 105 mm sag with forks flush
common_fixes.result: Controlled slow-speed bump absorption with only occasional controlled bottoming

bikes.summary: Only a dyno test exists for this generation; it measured about the same peak as one rival 450.

points.statement: On one dyno the 2022 model matched a rival 450's peak power.

bikes.summary: One first-impression test found the 250 XC-F air fork harsh on square edges and sharp chop at standard pressure, and the six-speed's big jump to sixth hard to engage.

points.statement: At standard pressure the air fork felt harsh on square edges and sharp chop and could not be softened without losing bottoming resistance.
Semi-close six-speed has a big jump to sixth that is hard to engage.

common_fixes.fix: 107 mm sag instead of 105
common_fixes.result: More stable with a lower rear on corner entry, slightly slower steering

bikes.summary: Little tester commentary exists beyond a dyno test. A few owners reported fuel pump failures, sometimes after long idling with little fuel.

points.statement: A few owners report the fuel pump fuse blowing or the pump dying; others had no issues.

common_fixes.fix: Replace pump and filter; keep enough fuel to cover the pump
common_fixes.result: Running again

bikes.generation: older-frame woods model with PDS rear
bikes.summary: Testers call the 450 XCF-W the smoothest KTM four-stroke: it lugs to very low rpm and finds traction where a motocross bike spins, at the cost of peak power from its quiet exhaust. The linkless PDS shock is valued for ground clearance and not snagging logs. The 2023 coil fork was too soft and pitchy at speed, and the 2024 closed-cartridge fork was a big improvement.

points.statement: Smoothest KTM four-stroke: lugs to very low rpm without bogging, builds steadily and finds traction where motocross bikes spin.
Quiet exhaust and tame tune cost peak power compared with the XC-F; an aftermarket exhaust recovers about half of what racers want.
Linkless PDS shock gives more ground clearance and nothing to snag on logs and rocks.
2023 fork was softer than a motocross setup, pitchy and divey at high speed; happiest under 30-40 mph.
The 2024 closed-cartridge fork was a major improvement over the 2023 fork.
Map switch, traction control and quickshifter are optional; the map light is hard to see in sun and buttons sit close together.

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket exhaust, then remap and cams
common_fixes.result: Exhaust recovers about half; mapping and cams the rest

bikes.summary: Testers found the FX 450 smooth off the bottom and strong through the middle with no surges, so it feels slower than it is. Its five-speed's tall first gear is the main complaint for trail riding, and the suspension needed more hold-up, especially in front, everywhere except slow rocky terrain.

points.statement: Smooth off the bottom, strong through the middle and still pulling at the limiter, with no surges; feels slower than it is.
Five-speed with a tall first gear for tight trails, and it runs out of gear on fast desert.
Needed more hold-up, especially at the front, everywhere except very slow rocky terrain.
Spoke nipples and rear sprocket bolts need frequent checks and the airbox-cover hook can snap when refitted.

common_fixes.fix: Gear down for trails, up for motocross
common_fixes.result: Better match to terrain

common_fixes.fix: Fit a sixth gear (cases accept it)
common_fixes.result: Usable top gear

bikes.summary: Little tester commentary exists: one dyno tester described linear, controllable delivery, and the five-speed's limits for fast desert still apply.

points.statement: Linear, controllable delivery.
Five-speed runs out of gear on fast desert; a sixth gear is the usual fix.

bikes.summary: Testers describe the FX 350 as closer to a mellow 450 than a 250F: only a few hp short of a 450, pulling a long way and easy to short-shift when tired, and it stalls less than a 450. Stock settings suit most vet tracks, and the 2025 frame needs no break-in.

points.statement: Feels like a mellow 450: only a few hp short, pulls a long way and can be short-shifted when tired.
Stalls less than a 450 when ridden low in the rpm off-road.
Stock settings suit most vet tracks; faster tracks need a few more clicks of fork compression.
2025 frame needs no break-in.

bikes.summary: One Australian test found the 2020 FE 450's stiffer frame more stable at speed and less harsh, while its spring fork was plush in the woods but too soft on a motocross track.

points.statement: Stiffer 2020 frame is more stable at speed and less harsh.
Spring fork is plush in the woods but too soft on a motocross track; the shock handles big hits better than the fork.

bikes.summary: Testers found the 2024 FE 450 smooth and easy with strong low-end grunt and good climbing, but heavier and more work in tight sections than the smaller FEs. The switch to a closed-cartridge fork made it firmer and less prone to bottoming.

points.statement: Smooth and easy with strong low-end grunt and good climbing, pulling from corners in second to fourth.
Feels heavier and needs more effort in tight sections than the FE 250/350; sometimes pushes the front.
New closed-cartridge fork is firmer and bottoms less than the previous open-cartridge fork.

bikes.generation: first generation (KTM XC-F based, air fork)
bikes.summary: The first EX 350F uses the KTM XC-F engine and chassis with a restrictive airbox, a plain header and no map switch, and testers found it weaker than the KTM out of tight uphill turns. The air fork was plush and most testers stayed near stock. Forged clamps caused front push until torqued higher.

points.statement: Weaker than the KTM out of tight turns; testers traced it to the airbox and plain header rather than the engine.
Stock fork plush; most testers stayed close to stock clickers.
Six-speed has a much lower first and taller third to fifth than the motocross box; sixth is unusable on a track.
Rim-lock spoke loosens quickly, plastic preload ring gets chewed, fuel cap clogs with dirt.

common_fixes.problem: Weak pull out of tight uphill turns
common_fixes.fix: KTM vented airbox cover (winglet removed)
common_fixes.result: Noticeably better pull; with no cover it pulled third cleanly

common_fixes.fix: Top clamp bolts 20 Nm, bottom 15 Nm
common_fixes.result: Push cured

common_fixes.problem: Third gear not usable on MX
common_fixes.result: Third usable

bikes.generation: first generation (KTM XC-F based, air fork)
bikes.summary: Testers measured a clear low-rpm dip and less power than the KTM, blamed on the closed airbox, missing map 2 and plain header. The suspension was firm early but short on progression, bottoming on big hits and blowing through at pro pace, with a soft, wallowy shock.

points.statement: Clear dip around 4,300-4,700 rpm and less power than the KTM 250 SX-F, blamed on the closed airbox, single map and plain header.
Fork is firm early but short on progression and bottoms on big fast hits; shock soft with some wallow; both ends blow through at pro pace.

common_fixes.fix: Higher fork air and 105-108 mm sag
common_fixes.result: Better hold-up and bottoming resistance, though valving stays soft

bikes.generation: first generation (KTM XC-F based, air fork)
bikes.summary: Only a shootout note exists: added fork air helped, but both ends still lacked bottoming resistance compared with rivals.

points.statement: Both ends lacked bottoming resistance compared with rival off-road 450s, even with added fork air.

bikes.summary: Testers found the 2024 EX 450F very stable at speed with playful, soft off-road suspension and a coil fork that stays more planted than the air fork as tracks get rough. Complaints centre on a Braktec clutch that drags unless fully pulled, poor cold starting in gear, missing protection and a rear tire short on side grip.

points.statement: Very stable in fifth gear on chop, with playful, soft off-road suspension.
Closed-cartridge coil fork stays more planted than the air fork as the track gets choppy; racier than the enduro fork on big hits and ruts.
Keeps motocross character: free-revving with strong mid-to-top but less bottom-end tractability than the EC enduro.
Braktec hydraulic clutch drags unless pulled fully in; the tester stalled four times.
Will not start in gear when cold, weak start button, no handguards or skid plate; 18-inch rear tire lacks side bite.

common_fixes.fix: Set the lever fully out
common_fixes.result: Less drag

bikes.summary: Testers find the EX 350F keeps a free-revving motocross character with less bottom-end tractability than the enduro EC, and its closed-cartridge fork handles big hits and ruts but is harsher on roots and loose rock.

points.statement: Closed-cartridge fork handles big hits, braking bumps and ruts well but is harsher on roots and loose rock than the enduro fork.
Free-revving with strong mid-to-top pull, but less bottom tractability and a less smooth throttle off idle than the EC models.

bikes.summary: One dyno tester described the 2024 EX 250F's power as long and linear with no hard hit, still revving out and suiting the wide-ratio six-speed.

points.statement: Long, linear power with no hard hit that still revs out; wide-ratio six-speed hides the gaps.

bikes.summary: Testers find the EC 450F smooth, mellow and less tiring than the cross-country EX, with better bottom-end tractability. Its open-cartridge fork is plush with low stiction on trails but soft at speed over big hits, and adding hold-up without harshness took a revalve.

points.statement: Smooth, mellow and less tiring, with better bottom-end tractability and a smoother throttle off idle than the EX.
Open-cartridge fork is plush with low stiction on trails but soft over big hits at speed; hard to add hold-up without harshness.

common_fixes.problem: Soft fork and shock at race pace
common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket revalve of fork and shock
common_fixes.result: Surprisingly good

common_fixes.fix: KTM XC-F silencer (fully open muffler caused low-rpm flame-outs)
common_fixes.result: Pulled harder

common_fixes.fix: Fork tubes flush in clamps; lower footpegs, taller seat, steering damper
common_fixes.result: Better balance and more open cockpit

bikes.summary: Testers find the TPI 300 XC-W smooth, mellow and easy to ride with excellent fuel economy, but lacking the bottom-end grunt and midrange pull of the old carbureted 300s, with a lean-feeling tune and light detonation on trailing throttle. The open-cartridge fork and progressive PDS shock are plush at low speed but dive, wallow and bottom, and suit riders up to about 170-180 lb. ECU replacements or reflashes and higher-compression heads are the most common engine fixes.

points.statement: Smooth, long and friendly powerband that is easy to ride at low speed.
Lacks the bottom-end grunt and midrange pull of earlier carbureted 300s; the stock map feels lean, with a weak spot in the midrange.
Light detonation can be heard at low rpm and on trailing throttle, worse on 87-octane fuel.
Good fuel range: about 33-40 mpg, roughly 50 miles racing or 60-65 miles trail riding per tank.
Open-cartridge fork and progressive PDS shock are plush at low speed but dive under braking, wallow and bottom, and are sprung for about 170-180 lb riders.
PDS is cushy in tight rocks, roots and logs but gets bouncy at speed compared with the linkage XC.
On 2020 bikes long climbs or descents without stopping made it run lean or rich until restarted; a software update fixed it.
Never premix an oil-injected TPI, prime the oil line after throttle-body work, and warm the engine before riding hard to avoid seizures.

common_fixes.problem: Lean, flat stock fueling and detonation
common_fixes.fix: Replacement ECU or stock-ECU reflash
common_fixes.result: Runs better throughout, detonation removed, big gain in power and torque

common_fixes.problem: Weak low end, especially at altitude
common_fixes.fix: High-compression head (with mountain insert) plus remap
common_fixes.result: More low-end grunt and midrange pull

common_fixes.fix: Rework suspension and run about 108-115 mm sag; 1/4 turn more high-speed compression
common_fixes.result: Better cornering and no blow-through on logs

common_fixes.fix: Heavier flywheel, high-compression head and reflash
common_fixes.result: Smoother part throttle and fewer stalls

common_fixes.problem: Bike delivered with power-valve adjuster screwed all the way in
common_fixes.fix: Back the adjuster out
common_fixes.result: Harder hit while keeping bottom-end chug

bikes.generation: TBI fuel injection, new frame, closed-cartridge coil fork
bikes.summary: Testers agree the TBI 300 XC-W lugs at very low rpm without stalling and delivers smooth, tractor-like low-to-mid torque, with a stronger midrange and longer rev than the TPI bike. The map switch was optional and testers say to buy it, though they disagree on how different the maps feel. The stiffer frame is planted at speed but deflects at low speed in rocks, the shorter coil fork makes the front sit low, and long-term testing found overheating, worse fuel range and fuel pickup problems.

points.statement: Lugs at very low rpm without bogging or stalling, with smooth, tractor-like low-to-mid torque.
Compared with the TPI bike it is mellow down low but far stronger in the midrange and revs much further.
Could not reliably pull third up steep, sandy climbs at altitude that the TPI bike handled.
Map switch was an optional extra; testers recommend buying it.
Stiffer frame is more planted and stable at speed but feels unsettled and deflects more over rocks at low speed.
Closed-cartridge coil fork is plush to mid-stroke and stable under braking but about 10 mm shorter, so the front sits low.
Riders under about 170 lb need few changes; riders over 200 lb find the shock too soft.
Runs hot and overheated within minutes of slow technical riding on a long-term bike.
Fuel range is worse than the TPI bike (about 22-32 mpg), and the high fuel pickup can starve the engine with fuel still in the tank.
On one test bike the oil-level light worked only intermittently and the bike ran out of oil, needing a new piston and rings.

common_fixes.fix: Run about 110 mm sag rather than moving the fork
common_fixes.result: Front lifted

common_fixes.fix: Lower swingarm pivot torque by 5-10%
common_fixes.result: Less rear stiffness

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket ECU opening the power valve slightly more
common_fixes.result: Woke the bike up

common_fixes.fix: 48-tooth rear sprocket
common_fixes.result: Tighter gaps but first and second very low

disagreements.topic: How different the two maps feel
sides: Difference mostly on top and hard to notice
Map 2 is a big step more aggressive and a handful in tight changes of direction

bikes.summary: One test found the TBI 250 XC-W has usable power across the range matched to its six-speed, with the damped clutch helping traction; map 2 is a big step more aggressive and can spin the rear unexpectedly.

points.statement: Usable power across the range, matched to the six-speed; damped clutch softens delivery for traction.
Map 2 is a big step more aggressive and can spin the rear tire unexpectedly.
250/300 suspension resisted bottoming and stayed consistent when pushed.

bikes.summary: Testers found the TPI 150 XC-W comes on sooner with much more bottom-end torque than the carbureted 150 but signs off early on top. Suspension is set soft for light trail riders, and it needed clearing out after idling.

points.statement: Comes on sooner with much more bottom-end torque and a strong midrange than the carbureted 150.
Signs off early on top.
Set soft for 140-160 lb trail riders; heavier fast riders need stiffer springs at both ends.
Needed clearing out after idling more than a minute or two.

bikes.summary: One test found the TBI 150 XC-W pulls well low on map 1 and builds linearly with little over-rev, with flawless fueling; suspension is softer and plusher than on the 250/300, and the undamped clutch means more shifting.

points.statement: Pulls well low on map 1 and builds linearly with no sharp hit; fueling described as flawless.
Softer and plusher than the 250/300.

bikes.summary: Testers call the TBI 300 XC bold and torquey, tractoring like a four-stroke in slow sections and crisp on top, with more torque than any earlier 300. The 2023 aggressive map was abrupt in technical terrain, and on rocky trails the stiff stock chassis and settings felt harsh, so one long-term owner tamed the power and revalved the suspension.

points.statement: Bold, torquey engine that tractors through slow sections and turns crisp on top; more torque than any earlier 300.
The 2023 aggressive map was abrupt and hard to control in technical terrain, and the mellow map a big step down.
Stiff stock chassis and settings feel harsh on rocky trails.

common_fixes.fix: Auto-clutch, slower-turning throttle cam, flywheel weights
common_fixes.result: More manageable power

common_fixes.fix: Revalve or replace suspension
common_fixes.result: Biggest single improvement

bikes.summary: Testers found the TPI 300 XC very smooth but lethargic off the bottom, with what sounded like low-rpm detonation. The linkage chassis is far more stable at speed than the XC-W but harsher in rocks, and owners riding motocross find the stock shock spring soft near 200 lb.

points.statement: Very smooth but lethargic off the bottom, with what sounded like low-rpm detonation.
Linkage rear is far more stable at speed and in big whoops than the XC-W, but harsher on rocks and hangs lower over logs.
Testers would prefer a spring fork's softer initial stroke for hidden rocks over the air fork.
Owners riding motocross near 200 lb find the stock 42 N/mm shock spring too soft.

common_fixes.fix: Race fuel in the mix and a power-valve tool
common_fixes.result: Livelier engine

common_fixes.fix: 48-50 N/mm spring, 105 mm race sag
common_fixes.result: Owners report better support

bikes.summary: One owner reported a 2020 250 XC TPI that spluttered at part throttle low to mid and ran rich; a magazine column suggested air-screw and ECU fixes.

points.statement: Spluttery at part throttle from low to mid rpm with a flat top and signs of rich running.

common_fixes.fix: Turn in the throttle-body air screw, get the latest dealer ECU settings, or a replacement ECU/reflash
common_fixes.result: Reported great results from a tested replacement ECU

bikes.summary: In a GNCC race test the carbureted 125 XC pulled well even when lugged in second or third, never felt narrow and needed less clutch than expected; it was raced with only sag set.

points.statement: Pulls well in second or third even when lugged, never feels narrow and needs less clutch than expected.

bikes.summary: One tester found the fork plush at first and able to handle all but the biggest motocross hits.

points.statement: Fork plush initially and handles all but the biggest track hits.

bikes.summary: Testers agree the TPI TE 300 makes lots of usable bottom and mid power and is almost impossible to stall, with low vibration and gentle brakes and clutch, though power tapers quickly past the middle.
