The open-cartridge fork is cushy in rocks but too soft for heavier or aggressive riders and dives under braking. One tester felt a lean tune with light detonation and found the map switch made little difference.

points.statement: Huge, usable bottom and mid power delivered linearly; very hard to stall and best ridden a gear high.
Power tapers quickly past the midrange.
Fork too soft for heavier or aggressive riders: dives under braking and bottoms on G-outs, even at maximum preload.
Spring suspension is cushy and excellent in rocks.
Map switch made a negligible difference; a slightly lean feel and occasional light detonation under low-rpm load were blamed on the emissions tune.
Low vibration and reliable electric start; brakes and clutch less grabby than the KTM's.
Slippery seat cover lets the rider slide back on climbs.
Injection improved fuel mileage over the carbureted version (about 7% at sea level, over 20% near 6,000 ft) and cut oil use.

common_fixes.problem: Fork dives and bottoms, left leg doing most work
common_fixes.fix: Revalve with rebalanced damping and 15 ml more oil
common_fixes.result: Bottoming fixed without losing plushness

common_fixes.fix: Replacement ECU
common_fixes.result: Better running and no detonation

bikes.summary: Testers describe the TBI TE 300 as milder at the bottom and stronger in the middle than the TE 250. Its coil fork is cushy at low speed but very soft overall, diving under hard braking, while the shock is good in rocks and stable at speed.

points.statement: Milder bottom and stronger midrange than the TE 250; the aggressive map surges near peak rather than hitting.
Coil fork is cushy at low speed but very soft overall, diving under hard braking and struggling on G-outs; more compression mostly kills low-speed comfort.
Shock is good in rocks and stable at speed.

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe and silencer
common_fixes.result: Crisper with more bottom-end feel

bikes.summary: One launch test found the TBI TE 250 snappy from the start and clearly stronger than the TE 150.

points.statement: Snappy from the start; much stronger than the TE 150.

bikes.summary: One launch test found the TBI TE 150 has a strong, four-stroke-like bottom end with two-stroke snap when the clutch is flicked.

points.statement: Strong, four-stroke-like bottom end with two-stroke snap on a clutch flick.

bikes.summary: One magazine found the TPI TX 300 top-end biased, with a soft spot around 7,000 rpm before a strong kick to sign-off, and ran the aggressive map all the time. Testers agree the fuel delivery is its weak spot: it cut out when whipped low on fuel and the in-tank pump occasionally failed. The air fork bottoms below about 144 psi.

points.statement: Top-end biased: soft spot around 7,000 rpm, then a strong kick from 8,000 rpm to sign-off; testers ran the aggressive map all the time.
Fuel delivery is the weak point: the engine can quit when low on fuel and leaned over, and the in-tank pump occasionally fails.
Below about 144 psi the fork bottoms on big hits; 102-108 mm sag is the sweet spot.
18-inch rear off-road tire is poor for motocross use.

common_fixes.fix: Aftermarket pipe
common_fixes.result: About 3 hp more at 7,500 and 9,000 rpm

common_fixes.fix: Raise the fork tubes in the clamps
common_fixes.result: Push cured

bikes.summary: One full test found suspension the main area to improve on the TBI TX 300, with off-road air-fork valving and shorter travel than the KTM 300 XC for a lower seat; its two maps range from mild to very aggressive.

points.statement: Suspension is the main area needing improvement.
Two bar-switch maps range from mild to very aggressive.

bikes.summary: Testers found the TPI EX 300 strong with spot-on throttle response but wanting a smoother bottom for slow trail, with lean spots until fully warm. Its air fork and shock felt stiff and harsh for trail riding and needed constant attention. It ships without a map switch, handguards or skid plate.

points.statement: Air fork and shock feel jarringly stiff for trail riding and deflect in fast chatter; they need constant attention.
Plenty of power and spot-on throttle response, but the bottom end could be smoother for slow technical trail and it runs lean until warm.
No handguards or skid plate, vulnerable exhaust and no map switch.

common_fixes.fix: Lower air pressure, more compression clicks out and slower rebound
common_fixes.result: Comfort with enough hold-up; shock still soft on big hits

common_fixes.fix: Slow the power-valve opening slightly (about a quarter turn)
common_fixes.result: Delivery suited to the rider

bikes.summary: Testers find the TBI EX 300 pulls from very low revs and can be lugged almost to idle, with most power bottom to mid and the TPI's lean surge mostly gone, though the power-valve tune feels conservative. It lacks a map switch, handguards and skid plate, its Braktec brakes fade sooner than Brembos, and testers note TPS recalibration and a high fuel pickup. Sag runs high stock, so testers shorten the shock or lower it.

points.statement: Pulls from very low revs and can be lugged almost to idle; most power is bottom to mid and the TPI's low-rpm lean surge is mostly gone.
Power-valve tune feels conservative.
Ships without a map switch, handguards or skid plate.
Braktec brakes fade faster than Brembo, especially the rear.
Throttle position sensor may need recalibrating every 15-20 hours; fuel pickup sits high and can starve the engine with fuel left.
Good balance, with occasional bottoming under heavy loads.

common_fixes.fix: Shorten the shock 1-3 mm internally; fork flush or slightly below in clamps
common_fixes.result: 100-105 mm sag; dropping the fork further cost front grip

common_fixes.fix: 14/50 to 14/52 (14/49 for fast terrain)
common_fixes.result: Better gear use

bikes.summary: Testers found the TPI EC 300 a little mellower than the carbureted bikes and lean-feeling until warm, but able to tractor through rough terrain. Its coil suspension is trail-oriented and soft for riders over about 170-175 lb, and its front brake is weaker than the KTM and Husqvarna units. Backing out the power-valve adjuster sharpens the midrange.

points.statement: Trail-oriented coil suspension is soft for riders over about 170-175 lb; even a light expert wanted more support on G-outs.
A little mellower than the carbureted bikes and slightly lean until warm, but tractors through rugged terrain.
Front brake is the weak point: firm lever but less stopping power than the KTM and Husqvarna siblings.
About 12 lb heavier than a PDS 300 XC-W.

common_fixes.fix: Back the power-valve adjuster out (about two turns)
common_fixes.result: Opens sooner with a stronger midrange

common_fixes.fix: Stiffer springs both ends or closed-cartridge kit
common_fixes.result: More support

common_fixes.fix: Replacement ECU
common_fixes.result: Ran better from the bottom up, no detonation

bikes.summary: Testers find the TBI EC 300 can crawl at almost closed throttle without stalling, with a stout bottom, crisp midrange and smooth, linear power that no longer lean-pops like the TPI, though it lacks some of the carburetor bikes' snap. It ships without a map switch, and its open-cartridge fork is less consistent than the KTM's and bottoms when pushed.

points.statement: Crawls at almost closed throttle without stalling; stout bottom and crisp midrange with smooth, linear delivery.
Smoother and more four-stroke-like than older carbureted 300s, which hit harder off the bottom.
Open-cartridge fork is less consistent and less plush over small bumps than the KTM's closed-cartridge fork and bottoms when pushed; fine for casual riding.
No map switch fitted; the optional switch plugs straight in (white for rock crawling, green for mud and open trail).
